U.S. FUEL PRICES have risen to their highest level since the war with Iran began as the renewed rise in crude prices is compounded by crack spreads still at near-record highs.  The combined cost of fuels and refining margins is now higher than it was in early April before the first of the ceasefires. So far this month the combined cost of U.S. crude ($92) and the 3-2-1 crack ($62) is higher than in May ($98 and $53) and April ($99 and $47). The intense upward pressure on fuel prices at wholesale level is putting upward pressure on prices at the pump, increasing costs for households and businesses, and playing into discontent about higher prices and the cost of living:

U.S. oil output flattens as shale revolution matures

U.S. oil production has remained essentially stable over the last year as the industry has focused on controlling costs and maintaining a disciplined approach to investment despite higher prices driven by war in the Middle East. 

Total crude and condensates production increased by just 136,000 barrels per day (b/d) or 1% in June compared with the same month a year earlier, according to data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration.  

Very modest growth is based on revised and more comprehensive data for 2025 from the U.S. Energy Information Administration published on September 1.  

Production from the Lower 48 states excluding federal waters in the Gulf of Mexico increased by less than 90,000 b/d in June compared with a year earlier, the slowest growth since the pandemic ...

OPEC crude production fell by 900,000 b/d last month to 19.9 mb/d, almost 10 mb/d below pre-war levels, and partly reversing the increase that followed the signing of the now-failed MOU. The decline was primarily driven by a 1.1 mb/d slump in Saudi output amid attacks on pipeline infrastructure, only partly offset by increases from Iraq, Kuwait, Nigeria and Venezuela, the latter reaching an eight-year high at 1.2 mb/d. (Source: Bloomberg production survey).
